jurisdiction.name: New York City
jurisdiction.notes: Five boroughs, each its own county: Manhattan (New York County), Brooklyn (Kings), Queens (Queens), the Bronx (Bronx) and Staten Island (Richmond), so county is left null. Most food-business licenses are filed through NYC Business (MyCity) and paid at the DCWP Licensing Center; construction runs through DOB NOW. The cabaret license was repealed in 2017 and the 2024 City of Yes zoning text lifted the remaining dancing restrictions for eating and drinking establishments; noise is now the main entertainment constraint. SLA applications are reviewed by one of 59 Community Boards.

permits.name: NYC Food Protection Certificate (required supervisor on every shift)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) – Health Academy
permits.notes: The Health Code requires a supervisor holding a NYC Food Protection Certificate on site during all hours of operation, so most restaurants certify two or three managers. The online course is free with a $24 in-person final exam; the in-person 15-hour class plus exam is $114. ServSafe and other national certificates do not satisfy the NYC requirement. The certificate never expires.

permits.name: DOHMH Food Service Establishment permit
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
permits.notes: Fee is $280 for most establishments, plus $25 if you make frozen desserts; the permit runs one year. You may legally open 22 days after submitting the application even before inspection, or call 212-676-1600 to request an earlier pre-permit inspection. Have the Food Protection Certificate holder, proof of workers' comp/disability coverage (or CE-200) and the sales tax certificate ready when you file. Bars serving only packaged snacks still need a permit if any food or ice handling occurs.
permits.stall_risk: Unannounced pre-permit inspections after day 22 catch missing hand sinks, pest-proofing gaps or no certified supervisor on shift; a failed inspection means a re-inspection and possibly a closure order. Do a mock inspection against the DOHMH checklist, or buy the $400 consultative inspection, before opening day.

permits.name: DOHMH plan review for a new or renovated kitchen (filed alongside DOB plans)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
permits.notes: Unlike most cities, NYC's Health Department plan review is optional: kitchen layouts are approved through the DOB filing and the Health Code is enforced at the pre-permit inspection. Submitting the floor plan, equipment schedule and finish schedule to DOHMH while DOB reviews the job catches sink, ventilation and pest-proofing issues before they are built. Restaurants doing sous-vide, curing or other specialized processes must also get a HACCP plan approved.

permits.name: Zoning use check (eating & drinking use, use group, Certificate of Occupancy match)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of City Planning (Zoning Resolution) / Department of Buildings
permits.notes: Restaurants and bars are permitted as of right in most commercial districts but not in residence districts, and the building's Certificate of Occupancy must list an eating and drinking use group (or allow it) for the floor you lease. The 2017 cabaret-law repeal and the 2024 City of Yes for Economic Opportunity text removed the old ban on dancing outside certain districts, so entertainment is now governed by venue size, occupancy and the Noise Code. Have an expediter or architect pull the CO and ZoLa zoning map before signing; a mismatch means an Alteration-CO filing.

permits.name: DOB work permit – Alteration (former Alt 2) or Alteration-CO (former Alt 1) via DOB NOW
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Buildings (DOB) – DOB NOW: Build
permits.notes: A registered architect or engineer files the job in DOB NOW. Work that changes use, egress or occupancy is an Alteration-CO (formerly Alt 1) and ends in a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy; a fit-out that keeps the existing use is an Alteration (formerly Alt 2). Plumbing (including the grease interceptor), mechanical/hood, sprinkler and electrical work are separate permits pulled by licensed trades. Filing fees scale with construction cost; professional certification can skip full plan exam but invites audits.
permits.stall_risk: Plan-exam objections and landlord-side issues (open violations, outdated CO, missing sign-offs on old jobs) routinely add 1–3 months. Run a DOB BIS/DOB NOW property profile before signing the lease and hire an expediter familiar with restaurant filings.

permits.name: Certificate of Occupancy / Temporary CO (change of use or occupancy)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Buildings (DOB)
permits.notes: New buildings and any change in use, egress or occupancy type need a new or amended CO; nobody may legally occupy the space until DOB issues the CO or a Temporary CO. DOB issues it only after all work is signed off, fees are paid, violations are resolved and other agencies (FDNY, DEP) have approved. Many restaurants open on a TCO, which must be renewed until the final CO is issued.
permits.stall_risk: Final sign-offs from every trade and agency are needed before the TCO, and one missing inspection (sprinkler, elevator, plumbing) holds the whole space. Track every sign-off on the job from day one and book inspections as soon as each trade finishes.

permits.name: Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation (PACO) – 75+ occupants
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Buildings (DOB)
permits.notes: Required wherever 75 or more members of the public gather indoors (or 200 outdoors, including rooftops) to eat or drink. DOB approves the PA plan (seating and egress layout) and does the first inspection; the certificate runs one year, and within that year you must obtain the FDNY Place of Assembly permit. Any change to seating layout requires an amended plan. Keep designs at 74 occupants if you want to avoid PA requirements entirely.
permits.stall_risk: The PA plan approval and inspection are separate from the alteration job and are often discovered late, after the space is built. File the PA application together with the alteration filing and design egress, exit signage and emergency lighting to the PA standard from the start.

permits.name: FDNY Public Assembly permit (annual)
permits.issuing_agency: Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) – Bureau of Fire Prevention
permits.notes: Once DOB issues the Place of Assembly Certificate of Operation, FDNY issues an annual Public Assembly permit based on its own inspection; the fee varies with the number of occupants and the term is at most one year. FDNY checks DOB-approved seating plans, posted occupancy, exits and that Certificate of Fitness holders (F-03 for indoor assembly, S-95 where there is a fire alarm) are on staff.

permits.name: FDNY Commercial Cooking System permit (hood and suppression)
permits.issuing_agency: Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) – Bureau of Fire Prevention
permits.notes: Required to operate fryers, char broilers, griddles, ranges, ovens and similar grease-producing appliances under a hood. The permit fee is $70, and acceptance-test fees for the fire-extinguishing system may be added. FDNY does a preliminary inspection and test after plan approval and installation, then annual inspections. Hood cleaning must be done by a company whose staff hold W-64/P-64 Certificates of Fitness, at least every three months.

permits.name: FDNY Certificates of Fitness for staff (F-03 assembly safety, fire guard, etc.)
permits.issuing_agency: Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY)
permits.notes: Places of assembly need an F-03 (or equivalent) holder on duty whenever open to the public, and buildings with fire alarms need S-95 coverage. Staff study the FDNY notice of examination and test at FDNY headquarters or online for some certificates. Certify at least two managers so every shift is covered before the FDNY Public Assembly inspection.

permits.name: DEP grease interceptor (sewer use rules for food service)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)
permits.notes: Every grease-generating business must install, operate and maintain a properly sized grease interceptor, installed by a licensed plumber under the DOB plumbing permit and sized per 15 RCNY §19-11. Food waste disposers are not allowed in commercial establishments. DEP inspects routinely; an undersized or unmaintained interceptor can draw penalties of up to $10,000 per day. Keep pumping and renderer receipts on site.

permits.name: DOB sign permit (installed by a licensed sign hanger)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Buildings (DOB)
permits.notes: Signs over 6 square feet or any illuminated sign need a DOB sign permit filed in DOB NOW: Build, and installation must be done or supervised by a DOB-licensed Master or Special Sign Hanger (Special covers signs up to 150 sq ft). Illuminated signs projecting beyond the building line need an annual permit, and electrical hookups need a separate electrical permit. Landmarked buildings and historic districts (much of SoHo, the West Village, parts of Brooklyn) also need Landmarks Preservation Commission approval first.

permits.name: Dining Out NYC sidewalk / roadway café license (DOT)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Transportation (DOT) – Dining Out NYC
permits.notes: Since 2024 DOT runs the permanent program that replaced DCWP sidewalk café licenses and the pandemic Open Restaurants setups. You need a ground-floor DOHMH-permitted food establishment; the four-year license fee was set at $1,050 for sidewalk or roadway ($2,100 for both), plus annual per-square-foot consent fees. Sidewalk cafés may operate year-round; roadway cafés only April 1 to November 29. DOT estimates up to six months for sidewalk and five for roadway approvals, including Community Board review; serving alcohol outside also needs an SLA alteration approval.

permits.name: Community Board liquor license review (committee appearance + stipulations)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Community Boards (advisory to the NYS Liquor Authority)
permits.notes: After your 30-day notice, the Community Board's SLA committee usually asks you to present your method of operation (hours, music, security, outdoor seating) and may negotiate stipulations that become license conditions. The board's recommendation is advisory but goes into the SLA record. Notice is also required 30 days before renewals, alterations and major ownership changes. Each board has its own questionnaire and meeting calendar, so check it before sending notice.
permits.stall_risk: Boards meet monthly and may hold an application over if neighbors object, which can push the SLA filing by a month or more. Contact the committee chair early, bring letters of support, and offer reasonable stipulations (closing hours, closed windows for music) up front.

permits.name: NYC Noise Code compliance for commercial music (amplified sound / live music)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Environmental Protection (DEP)
permits.notes: NYC has no entertainment or cabaret license, but music from restaurants, bars and hotels must meet the Noise Code limits measured inside neighboring homes and on the street, and DEP issues violations on 311 complaints. Amplified sound outdoors (sidewalk cafés, rooftops) generally needs an NYPD sound device permit. DEP publishes guidance on acoustic products and a commercial music variance process. Soundproof before opening if residents live above or next door.

permits.name: NYC Hotel Room Occupancy Tax registration (Certificate of Authority)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Finance
permits.notes: Hotel operators must register within three days after guests begin renting rooms, and Finance issues a Certificate of Authority within five days that must be displayed. The city hotel tax (a percentage of the rent plus a flat $1.00–$2.00 per room per night on most rooms) sits on top of NYS sales tax and the NYS $1.50 per unit per day hotel unit fee, both collected by the State Tax Department. Stays of 180+ consecutive days by permanent residents are exempt.

permits.name: DCWP Hotel license (Safe Hotels Act, Local Law 104 of 2024)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP)
permits.notes: Since May 2025 every NYC hotel needs a two-year DCWP license expiring September 30 of even years; the fee is $350 for a full term and is prorated ($87.50–$437.50) depending on when you apply, plus a 2% card convenience fee. The application must document staffing, front-desk coverage, room-cleaning and safety procedures required by the Safe Hotels Act. Hotels must also register annually with HPD by September 1.

permits.name: DOHMH Mobile Food Vendor license (individual vendor ID)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (applications at the DCWP Licensing Center)
permits.notes: Every person who works on a cart or truck needs this personal license: $50 for two years plus $53 for the required Mobile Food Vendor food protection course (veterans pay no license fee). Apply in person by appointment at the DCWP Licensing Center. There is no waiting list for the vendor license itself, and holding one is what makes you eligible for the supervisory-license waiting lists.

permits.name: DOHMH Mobile Food Vending Unit permit (cart / truck) – supervisory license waitlist
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
permits.notes: Each cart or truck needs a unit permit: $200 for a two-year full-term permit when food is prepared on board ($75 pre-packaged), or $35/$15 for a seasonal April–October permit. Under Local Law 18 of 2021 a new full-term citywide or non-Manhattan permit requires a supervisory license, which is only offered from DOHMH waiting lists; from July 2026 the city is releasing at least 2,200 supervisory licenses a year for five years, first to people on the 2022 lists. The unit must pass inspection within six months of applying and operate from a permitted commissary.
permits.stall_risk: The permit cap and supervisory waitlist are the single biggest barrier to launching a NYC food truck; new entrants can wait years, and renting another holder's permit is illegal. Get the vendor license now to join the next waitlist, and meanwhile operate on private property, at markets, or on a seasonal permit.

permits.name: Commercial Rent Tax registration (Manhattan south of 96th Street)
permits.issuing_agency: NYC Department of Finance
permits.notes: Only applies if your premises are in Manhattan south of the center line of 96th Street and annual base rent is at least $250,000; tenants paying over $200,000 must still file a return. The effective rate is 3.9% of base rent after the 35% reduction, and a small-business credit exempts tenants with total income of $5 million or less and base rent under $500,000. Annual returns are due June 20; skip this item entirely outside that zone.
